children: The European Union said Temu could be in breach of the bloc's rules over how the company handles what regulators consider illegal products sold on its platform, after imposing a nearly $220 million fine on the company earlier this year.

In its preliminary findings, the European Commission said Tuesday that measures it put in place to tackle illegal products sold on its platform were ineffective, including what it called a "weak" content moderation system and ineffective sanctions.

It is the latest warning shot the EU has fired at the Chinese-owned e-commerce group as it has started enforcing the Digital Services Act, which obliges large platforms like Temu to do more to protect consumers online against what officials see as a raft of digital ills from hate speech to counterfeit goods.

"The preliminary findings against Temu mark another step towards making the online world safer," Henna Virkkunen, the EU's tech commissioner, said in a statement. The PDD Holdings-owned company could face a fine of up to 6% of its annual worldwide turnover if officials decide it is falling foul of the rules. The commission previously fined Alibaba's AliExpress 550 million euros--equivalent to around $604.9 million--in July over product safety concerns and started investigating Shein in February after French regulators said they had found sex dolls resembling children listed for sale on the platform in 2025.

The commission--the EU's executive arm--started a broad investigation into Temu under the DSA in 2024. It fined Temu 200 million euros in May this year, saying that a 2024 risk assessment the company had to carry out as part of its DSA obligations fell short of the rulebook's standards. Temu said at the time the commission's investigation related to a historic assessment and has since submitted a new plan to EU officials to comply with that part of the law.

In this part of the probe, officials said that Temu's content moderation system appears to focus on information on a product's listing and on compliance with its own terms rather than the safety of the product itself and that sanctions are imposed on individual stores within the website, meaning that retailers can keep selling through other stores if one is penalized.
Temu now has a chance to respond to the commission's initial findings before they wrap up their investigation, the EU said.
